mn2:1.2: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
mn2:1.3: There the Blessed One addressed the monks:
mn2:1.5: “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
mn2:2.1: “Monks, I will teach you the discourse on the restraint of all taints. Listen and attend closely to what I shall say.”
mn2:2.2: “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
mn2:2.4: “Monks, it is by knowing and seeing that I say there is the destruction of the taints, not by not knowing and not seeing.
mn2:3.1: And what, monks, is to be known and seen for the destruction of the taints?
mn2:3.3: When one attends unwisely, unarisen taints arise, and arisen taints increase.
mn2:3.4: When one attends wisely, unarisen taints do not arise, and arisen taints are abandoned.
mn2:4.1: There are taints to be abandoned by seeing, taints to be abandoned by restraint, taints to be abandoned by using, taints to be abandoned by enduring, taints to be abandoned by avoiding, taints to be abandoned by removing, and taints to be abandoned by developing.
mn2:5.0: 1. Taints to be Abandoned by Seeing
mn2:5.1: And what, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by seeing?
mn2:5.2: Here, monks, an uninstructed worldling—who has no regard for the noble ones, is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma, and has no regard for true persons, is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma—
mn2:5.3: does not understand what should be attended to and what should not be attended to.
mn2:5.4: Not understanding, they attend to what should not be attended to and do not attend to what should be attended to.
mn2:6.1: And what, monks, should not be attended to but is attended to?
mn2:6.2: When one attends to something, unarisen sensual taint arises, and arisen sensual taint increases;
mn2:6.3: unarisen taint of being arises, and arisen taint of being increases;
mn2:6.4: unarisen taint of ignorance arises, and arisen taint of ignorance increases—
mn2:6.5: these are what should not be attended to but are attended to.
mn2:6.6: And what, monks, should be attended to but is not attended to?
mn2:6.7: When one attends to something, unarisen sensual taint does not arise, and arisen sensual taint is abandoned;
mn2:6.8: unarisen taint of being does not arise, and arisen taint of being is abandoned;
mn2:6.9: unarisen taint of ignorance does not arise, and arisen taint of ignorance is abandoned—
mn2:6.10: these are what should be attended to but are not attended to.
mn2:7.1: When one attends to what should not be attended to and does not attend to what should be attended to, unarisen taints arise and arisen taints increase.
mn2:7.2: They attend unwisely in this way:
mn2:7.3: ‘Was I in the past? Was I not in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what was I in the past?’
mn2:7.4: ‘Shall I be in the future? Shall I not be in the future? What shall I be in the future? How shall I be in the future? Having been what, what shall I be in the future?’
mn2:7.5: Or they are inwardly perplexed about the present:
mn2:7.6: ‘Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? Where has this being come from? Where will it go?’
mn2:8.1: When one attends unwisely in this way, one of six views arises in them.
mn2:8.2: The view ‘I have a self’ arises in them as true and established;
mn2:8.3: or the view ‘I have no self’ arises in them as true and established;
mn2:8.4: or the view ‘It is by self that I perceive self’ arises in them as true and established;
mn2:8.5: or the view ‘It is by self that I perceive not-self’ arises in them as true and established;
mn2:8.6: or the view ‘It is by not-self that I perceive self’ arises in them as true and established;
mn2:8.7: or else they have this view:
mn2:8.8: ‘This self of mine, which speaks and feels and experiences here and there the result of good and bad actions, is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same just like that forever.’
mn2:8.9: This is called a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a contortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views.
mn2:8.10: Fettered by the fetter of views, the uninstructed worldling is not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; they are not freed from suffering, I say.
mn2:8.11: But a noble disciple who is learned, who has regard for the noble ones, is skilled and disciplined in their Dhamma, who has regard for true persons, is skilled and disciplined in their Dhamma—
mn2:9.1: understands what should be attended to and what should not be attended to.
mn2:9.2: Understanding, they do not attend to what should not be attended to and attend to what should be attended to.
mn2:9.3: And what, monks, should not be attended to but is not attended to?
mn2:9.4: When one attends to something, unarisen sensual taint does not arise, and arisen sensual taint is abandoned;
mn2:10.1: unarisen taint of being does not arise, and arisen taint of being is abandoned;
mn2:10.2: unarisen taint of ignorance does not arise, and arisen taint of ignorance is abandoned—
mn2:10.3: these are what should not be attended to but are not attended to.
mn2:10.4: And what, monks, should be attended to and is attended to?
mn2:10.5: When one attends to something, unarisen sensual taint does not arise, and arisen sensual taint is abandoned;
mn2:10.6: unarisen taint of being does not arise, and arisen taint of being is abandoned;
mn2:10.7: unarisen taint of ignorance does not arise, and arisen taint of ignorance is abandoned—
mn2:10.8: these are what should be attended to and are attended to.
mn2:10.9: When one does not attend to what should not be attended to and attends to what should be attended to, unarisen taints do not arise and arisen taints are abandoned.
mn2:10.10: They attend wisely in this way:
mn2:10.11: ‘This is suffering’; ‘This is the origin of suffering’; ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’
mn2:11.1: When one attends wisely in this way, three fetters are abandoned:
mn2:11.2: identity view, doubt, and clinging to rules and observances.
mn2:11.3: These are called the taints to be abandoned by seeing.
mn2:12.0: 2. Taints to be Abandoned by Restraint
mn2:12.1: And what, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by restraint?
mn2:12.2: Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, dwells restrained in the faculty of the eye. When the faculty of the eye is unrestrained, taints, vexation, and fever might arise; but there are no such taints when the faculty of the eye is restrained.
mn2:12.3: Reflecting wisely, they dwell restrained in the faculty of the ear ...
mn2:12.4: Reflecting wisely, they dwell restrained in the faculty of the nose ...
mn2:12.5: Reflecting wisely, they dwell restrained in the faculty of the tongue ...
mn2:12.6: Reflecting wisely, they dwell restrained in the faculty of the body ...
mn2:12.7: Reflecting wisely, they dwell restrained in the faculty of the mind.
mn2:12.8: When the faculty of the mind is unrestrained, taints, vexation, and fever might arise; but there are no such taints when the faculty of the mind is restrained.
mn2:12.9: When restraint is lacking, taints, vexation, and fever might arise; but there are no such taints when there is restraint.
mn2:12.10: These are called the taints to be abandoned by restraint.
mn2:13.0: 3. Taints to be Abandoned by Using
mn2:13.1: And what, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by using?
mn2:13.2: Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, uses the robe only for warding off cold, for warding off heat, for warding off the touch of gadfly, mosquito, wind, sun, and creeping things; only for the purpose of covering the parts of the body.
mn2:13.3: Reflecting wisely, they use almsfood not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for fattening, not for beautification, but only for the maintenance and nourishment of this body, for allaying hunger, and for assisting the holy life, thinking: ‘Thus I shall terminate old feelings and not arouse new feelings, and I shall be healthy and blameless and dwell at ease.’
mn2:14.1: Reflecting wisely, they use lodging only for warding off cold, for warding off heat, for warding off the touch of gadfly, mosquito, wind, sun, and creeping things; only for protection from the inclemencies of weather and for the enjoyment of seclusion.
mn2:15.1: Reflecting wisely, they use medicines and requisites for curing the sick only for warding off painful feelings and for the sake of good health.
mn2:16.1: When one does not use these things wisely, taints, vexation, and fever might arise; but there are no such taints when one uses them wisely.
mn2:16.2: These are called the taints to be abandoned by using.
mn2:17.0: 4. Taints to be Abandoned by Enduring
mn2:17.1: And what, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by enduring?
mn2:17.2: Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, is one who endures cold, heat, hunger, and thirst; the touch of gadfly, mosquito, wind, sun, and creeping things; ill-spoken, unwelcome words; and bodily feelings that are painful, racking, sharp, piercing, disagreeable, distressing, and menacing to life.
mn2:18.1: When one does not endure these things wisely, taints, vexation, and fever might arise; but there are no such taints when one endures them wisely.
mn2:18.2: These are called the taints to be abandoned by enduring.
mn2:19.0: 5. Taints to be Abandoned by Avoiding
mn2:19.1: And what, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by avoiding?
mn2:19.2: Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, avoids a wild elephant, a wild horse, a wild bull, a wild dog, a snake, a stump, a thorn patch, a pit, a precipice, a sewer, a cesspool.
mn2:19.3: They avoid sitting in unsuitable seats, wandering in unsuitable resorts, and associating with bad friends, for wise companions in the holy life might suspect them of evil conduct.
mn2:19.4: When one does not avoid these things wisely, taints, vexation, and fever might arise; but there are no such taints when one avoids them wisely.
mn2:19.5: These are called the taints to be abandoned by avoiding.
mn2:20.0: 6. Taints to be Abandoned by Removing
mn2:20.1: And what, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by removing?
mn2:20.2: Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought; they abandon it, remove it, do away with it, and annihilate it. They do not tolerate an arisen thought of ill will ... an arisen thought of cruelty ... whatever bad, unskillful qualities have arisen; they abandon them, remove them, do away with them, and annihilate them.
mn2:20.3: When one does not remove these things wisely, taints, vexation, and fever might arise; but there are no such taints when one removes them wisely.
mn2:20.4: These are called the taints to be abandoned by removing.
mn2:21.0: 7. Taints to be Abandoned by Developing
mn2:21.1: And what, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by developing?
mn2:21.2: Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and ripens in relinquishment;
mn2:21.3: they develop the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena ...
mn2:21.4: they develop the enlightenment factor of energy ...
mn2:21.5: they develop the enlightenment factor of rapture ...
mn2:21.6: they develop the enlightenment factor of tranquility ...
mn2:21.7: they develop the enlightenment factor of concentration ...
mn2:21.8: they develop the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and ripens in relinquishment.
mn2:21.9: When one does not develop these things wisely, taints, vexation, and fever might arise; but there are no such taints when one develops them wisely.
mn2:21.10: These are called the taints to be abandoned by developing.
mn2:22.1: When, monks, for a monk, the taints to be abandoned by seeing are abandoned by seeing, the taints to be abandoned by restraint are abandoned by restraint, the taints to be abandoned by using are abandoned by using, the taints to be abandoned by enduring are abandoned by enduring, the taints to be abandoned by avoiding are abandoned by avoiding, the taints to be abandoned by removing are abandoned by removing, the taints to be abandoned by developing are abandoned by developing—
mn2:22.2: this is called a monk who dwells restrained with regard to all taints, who has cut off craving, untied the fetters, and, by completely understanding conceit, has made an end of suffering.
mn2:22.3: This is what the Blessed One said.
mn2:22.4: The monks were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
mn2:22.5: The Discourse on All Taints is finished.
